item.title: Transversal Fanout for Fault Tolerant Distributed Quantum Computing: Analysis and Application
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Constructs transversal distributed logical fanout and global controlled-Z (GCZ) operations across encoded code blocks to minimize non-local communication and entanglement overhead.

Grade 0.499 · 3.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Seng W. Loke

Asks

How can logical fanout operations across remote nodes in distributed quantum computers be implemented fault-tolerantly with reduced non-local communication overhead?

But

Theoretical and architectural analysis; illustrated specifically on Bivariate Bicycle code blocks.

Tools

transversal logical operations · Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes · distributed quantum circuit construction · resource-cost analysis

Abstract

We study a resource-efficient approach for implementing logical fanout operations in fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing using transversal operations on quantum error-correcting code blocks. Logical fanout, comprising multiple controlled-NOT operations from a common control qubit to target qubits located at remote nodes, is an important primitive for distributed quantum computation but can require substantial non-local communication when implemented directly between encoded blocks. We exploit the structure of encoded blocks and the availability of transversal logical operations to construct distributed fanout circuits that reduce the required non-local operations while preserving the logical action of the fanout operation. The construction is developed for encoded quantum information and illustrated using Bivariate Bicycle (BB)-code blocks. We analyze the resulting physical gate, entanglement, circuit-depth, and ancilla requirements. The approach provides a systematic method for implementing large logical fanout operations across distributed error-corrected quantum processors. Also, we study a distributed implementation of the global gate GCZ involving logical qubits (encoded using BB-code blocks), exploiting the concurrency in transversal distributed fanouts.

item.title: First fault-tolerant quantum memory demonstration for a generalized superfast encoding
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Even-distance Generalized Superfast Encoding maintains constant stabilizer weights of 4 or 6, exhibiting a quantum memory pseudo-threshold crossing near physical depolarizing error rate p≈4×10−3.

Grade 0.492 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · James Brown, Kenny Heitritter

Figure

Logical error rate per round per logical qubit versus physical error rate p. The [[64,8,8]] code suppresses errors faster than the [[48,8,6]] code below their projected crossing point near p≈4×10−3.

Asks

Can a fermion-to-qubit mapping achieve fault-tolerant quantum memory with threshold-like error suppression under circuit-level noise?

Before

Generalized Superfast Encoding was restricted to error detection or odd-distance constructions with weight-6 stabilizers (Brown et al. 2024), with no fault-tolerant quantum memory threshold observed.

But

Circuit-level depolarizing noise simulations only; evaluated on two code instances ([[48,8,6]] and [[64,8,8]]); requires N>d.

Tools

Generalized Superfast Encoding (GSE) · AlphaSyndrome circuit scheduling · Relay-BP message-passing decoder · Stim Monte Carlo simulation · Bare-ancilla syndrome extraction

Abstract

The Generalized Superfast Encoding (GSE) is a fermion-to-qubit mapping that has error-correcting/detecting properties. To this point, all demonstrations have been relegated to error-detection only, as no fault-tolerance under circuit-level noise has been observed. Here, we introduce an even-distance d constant stabilizer-weight GSE where each of N modes is assigned a d-qubit block arranged on a ring. The resulting stabilizer generators have constant weight 4 or 6 for any even distance d. Furthermore, the full stabilizer set of this construction can always be partitioned into four qubit-wise commuting groups, which enables compact syndrome-extraction scheduling. We simulate quantum memory experiments under circuit-level depolarizing noise for two instances of this code, [[48,8,6]] and [[64,8,8]] and the threshold is observed to be ≈4×10⁻³. This is, to our knowledge, the first fault-tolerant quantum-memory characterization of a fermion-mapping with threshold-like scaling.

item.title: Asymmetric quantum error correction efficiently tackles application-specific noise effects
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Asymmetric (5,3) quantum parity code with 15 physical qubits matches the optimization performance of the symmetric (5,5) code requiring 25 qubits because QAOA objective degrades significantly more under bit flips than phase flips.

Grade 0.485 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Abhishek Yadav, Peter K. Schuhmacher, Michael Epping

Figure

Residual cost deviation Δ plotted against physical error probability p under d=2 layer-level noise for uncoded QAOA and various quantum parity code configurations (n1,n2).

Asks

How do asymmetric bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise channels affect QAOA performance across different circuit decompositions, and can asymmetric quantum error correction exploit this asymmetry?

But

Simulated on a 6-qubit flight-gate assignment problem; syndrome extraction circuit noise and gate-level QEC fault-tolerance overhead not directly modeled in the QEC evaluation.

Tools

Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) · Quantum Parity Code (QPC) · Exact density-matrix simulation · Layer-level and gate-level Pauli noise models

Abstract

Noise is a major challenge for current quantum computers. It can be broadly categorized into bit-flip and phase-flip errors. These two types do not necessarily affect the executed algorithm, thus also the application, in the same way. We illustrate this general effect for the example of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) applied to a small instance of the flight-gate assignment (FGA) problem. We compare bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise under both layer-level and gate-level noise models, using two circuit decompositions of the same ideal QAOA unitary: a CNOT-based decomposition and a native-R_ZZ decomposition. In the simulations, bit-flip noise produces the larger degradation in the performance of the quantum optimization. The asymmetry is most visible in the layer-level and native-R_ZZ simulations. We explain this by how the errors affect mixing, final measurements, and how they propagate inside the circuit. We then exploit these insights to tackle noise particularly efficiently using asymmetric error-correcting codes. As an illustration, we use the quantum parity code (QPC), a generalization of the 9-qubit Shor code, and show that a smaller asymmetric code can achieve nearly the same improvement as a larger symmetric choice. This demonstrates that error-correction resources should be assigned not only according to physical error rates, but also according to how strongly each error channel affects the application. As a result, asymmetric quantum error correction proves useful even in cases where the noise model is symmetric. Finally, we discuss how information about the noise obtained through calibration can be exploited in our approach.

item.title: Computing 256-bit elliptic curve discrete logarithms in 26 days on a fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computer with 20,000 qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Solving the ECDLP on 𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚙𝟸𝟻𝟼𝚔𝟷 requires 19,397 physical trapped-ion qubits and 25.7 days for a 63% success probability per attempt, executing 40⋅106 Toffoli gates over 1457 logical qubits.

Grade 0.484 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Thomas Häner, Felix Tripier, Jacob Young, Michael Naehrig, Andrii Maksymov, Safwan Alam, Dmitri Maslov, Matthew Parrott, Yvette de Sereville, Jordan Sullivan, Mark Webster, Nicolas Delfosse, John Gamble, Martin Roetteler

Figure

Physical layout of the 19,397-qubit 𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚙𝟸𝟻𝟼𝚔𝟷 processor, showing 69 memory blocks, 4 CCZ magic-state factories, edge-packed cat-state factories, and Bell-state routing channels.

Asks

How many physical qubits and how much runtime does a fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computer need to compute 256-bit elliptic curve discrete logarithms under realistic noise, transport, and loss constraints?

Before

Prior trapped-ion estimates required 1.2 million to 9.4 million physical qubits; recent generic-architecture estimates needed 60⋅106 Toffolis (Schrottenloher 2026).

But

Assumes physical two-qubit gate error rate p=10−4, single-qubit error rate 10−5, swap-loss with pleak=p/10 and ploss=p/1000. Success probability lower-bounded assuming all 69 memory blocks remain active throughout full runtime.

Tools

Walking Cat architecture · quantum LDPC codes ([[102,22,9]] and [[66,4,10]]) · Eastinthillation CCZ factory · depth-one CCZ injection · logical CliNR frame clearing

Abstract

One of the strengths of our recently proposed Walking Cat Architecture for a trapped-ion quantum computer is that it is straightforward to extend and optimize for a specific application. As a proof-of-concept, here we present such optimizations for solving the 256-bit elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP) on secp256k1, which is the elliptic curve used by blockchain technologies such as Bitcoin, using Shor's algorithm. We optimize the circuits from Schrottenloher's recent work and arrive at a logical quantum circuit for solving the ECDLP using about 1450 qubits and 40·10⁶ Toffoli gates, with a rigorous lower bound on the logical-level success probability that holds with confidence at least 1-2⁻¹²⁸. Using our compilation toolchain with manual optimization of the logical layout and integrated routing, we produce estimates for the logical measurement depth and the required number of physical qubits by compiling all components to measurement schedules that obey the architectural constraints. A key ingredient is a fast CCZ magic-state factory and a depth-one CCZ state injection, reducing the execution time of CCZ gates by a factor of 31. We increase the logical-measurement parallelism using non-overlapping cat-based measurements in parallel, and we leverage the recently proposed logical CliNR protocol to speed up Clifford operations. To reduce the qubit overhead, we introduce a more efficient loss correction protocol, design a layout that allows us to recycle the CliNR ancilla qubits, and provision reusable cat-state resources according to the circuit's peak measurement parallelism. All results and optimizations combined, we conclude that a trapped-ion quantum computer based on our architecture can solve the ECDLP on secp256k1 in approximately 25.7 days using 19,397 physical qubits with an estimated success probability of 63%.

item.title: From Bits to Qubits: The Theory and Practice of Quantum Data Encoding
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Surveys quantum data encoding methods across state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM, and block-encoding, synthesizing circuit size, depth, and fault-tolerant gate counts.

Grade 0.475 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Xiao-Ming Zhang, Arthur G. Rattew, Bujiao Wu, Georgios Styliaris, Xiaoming Sun, Bálint Koczor, Xiao Yuan

Figure

Three core access models mapping classical vectors and matrices to quantum operations: quantum state preparation, QRAM, and block-encoding.

Asks

How can deterministic classical data be compiled into quantum representations under minimal circuit depth, gate counts, and non-Clifford resources?

But

Restricted to deterministic, fully known classical data in the standard qubit circuit model with all-to-all or binary-tree connectivity; excludes sampled distributions and continuous variables.

Tools

uniformly controlled rotations (UCR) · Schmidt decomposition · QRAM bucket-brigade architecture · linear combination of unitaries (LCU) · block-encoding

Abstract

Encoding classical data into quantum systems is a foundational step in the execution of nearly all quantum algorithms, and a critical bottleneck in realizing practical quantum advantage. This review provides a comprehensive account of the concepts, algorithms, and practical considerations associated with quantum data encoding. We trace the development from its early conceptual foundations to recent advances, considering commonly used access models, such as quantum state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM and block encoding. We survey the circuit size, depth, space-time tradeoffs, as well as non-Clifford resources required for fault-tolerant implementation. We also discuss the roles of different access models in quantum algorithms. Special attention is given to structured data, such as sparse data, Boolean functions and data represented by tensor networks. This review bridges theory and applications, serving both as a pedagogical guide for newcomers and as a reference for active researchers. We also highlight the pivotal role of quantum data encoding in quantum computing and provide insights into future directions that will enable quantum advantage.

item.title: From NISQ to Fault-Tolerance: Applications and Algorithmic Benchmarks for Spin Qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Compiling Parity Twine to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits reduces the physical exchange-pulse count by more than 22% for QFT and up to 34% for QAOA compared to baseline compilation schemes.

Grade 0.455 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Frederik Lohof, Florian Ginzel, Wolfgang Lechner

Figure

Physical exchange-pulse count and Twine/Fowler pulse count ratio as a function of device length L for the quantum Fourier transform.

Asks

How do algorithmic benchmarks and simulation routines scale from NISQ to fault-tolerance when mapped directly to physical exchange-pulse sequences on exchange-only spin qubit QPUs?

But

Analytical and numerical compilation models; assumes single-pulse error rates p≈1.5×10−4, readout error pm≈0.01, and T2≈19.3 μs.

Tools

Parity Twine compilation · exchange-only (EO) spin qubits · pulse-level scheduling with exclusion radius · surface code QEC / lattice surgery error modeling

Abstract

Motivated by recent breakthroughs in the development of spin-based quantum processing units based on exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, we provide a roadmap for the implementation of quantum algorithms on the EO platform, ranging from the NISQ to the fault-tolerant era. To provide an algorithm-driven perspective on the scaling of quantum chips, we consider a range of applications targeting different stages of hardware maturity and formulate requirements for a successful realization. We show that the compilation method Parity Twine perfectly complements the hardware's capabilities to perform tasks such as the quantum Fourier transform or QAOA. Furthermore, we describe an error detection technique native to Parity Twine, which EO qubits can leverage in a unique and advantageous way to improve algorithm performance. Finally, since both near-term algorithmic benchmarks and a long-term perspective can be found in digital quantum simulation, we specifically discuss the fermionic fast Fourier transform and the simulation of Fermi-Hubbard models. The latter is explicitly discussed in the context of quantum error correction and a partially fault-tolerant realization. By providing detailed resource estimates and identifying scaling bottlenecks on each level, our work offers a quantitative perspective on EO-based quantum computing and will inform future hardware design choices.

item.title: Toward Fault-Tolerant Variational Optimization: QAOA under [[4,2,2]] Error Detection
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Ancilla-mediated inter-block logical RZZ gate enables multi-block [[4,2,2]] error detection for QAOA Max-Cut. Encoded circuits maintain higher ground-state probability than unencoded baselines up to noise rate p=0.03 under grid-routed two-qubit depolarizing noise and up to p=0.04 with all-to-all connectivity.

Grade 0.448 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Matteo Robert Child, Emanuele Dri, Giacomo Vitali, Chiara Vercellino, Alberto Leporati

Figure

Post-selection rate (left) and post-selected ground-state probability (right) versus noise error probability p for single-qubit (top) and two-qubit (bottom) depolarizing noise channels under all-to-all and grid-routed topologies.

Asks

How can multi-block [[4,2,2]] error detection be implemented for QAOA Max-Cut circuits using non-transversal inter-block two-qubit rotations?

But

Numerical simulation on a single 4-vertex cycle graph C4. Post-selection acceptance rate drops exponentially with circuit depth and error rates.

Tools

[[4,2,2]] quantum error-detection code · QAOA · Cirq and qsimcirq · syndrome measurement post-selection

Abstract

We present a partially fault-tolerant implementation of QAOA based on the [[4,2,2]] error-detection code, targeting the Max-Cut problem on a square graph. Our main contribution is a novel ancilla-mediated logical R_ZZ gate enabling interactions between qubits in different [[4,2,2]] blocks. We evaluate unencoded and encoded circuits under five noise models, with both all-to-all and grid-routed connectivity, using the Cirq and qsimcirq frameworks with parallel CPU execution. Post-selection on stabilizer measurements consistently improves the probability of sampling optimal bitstrings, with five measurements providing the strongest benefit. These results support error-detection as a practical near-term strategy for improving the quality of variational quantum algorithms.

item.title: Quantum bivariate bicycle codes with weight-8 checks surpassing the BB benchmark
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Weight-8 bivariate bicycle codes yield [[144,6,d≥15]], [[144,10,12]], [[144,16,10]], and [[72,14,8]] with kd2/n=12.44. All have exact even dimension k=2dim⁡R/(A,B) and dX=dZ.

Grade 0.439 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Liangdong Lu, Ruipan Yang, Guanmin Guo

Figure

Logical error rate pL versus physical error rate p in a 6-round circuit-level memory experiment with BP-OSD decoding. Weight-8 codes exhibit a pseudo-threshold of ≈0.1%, compared to ≈0.4% and ≈0.2% for weight-6 reference codes.

Asks

Can bivariate bicycle codes with weight-8 checks be constructed and certified systematically to surpass the (n,k,d) performance of standard weight-6 bivariate bicycle codes?

Before

Flagship weight-6 bivariate bicycle code reached [[144,12,12]] with kd2/n=12, and length-72 reference was [[72,12,6]] with kd2/n=6 (Bravyi et al. 2024).

But

Circuit-level memory simulations assume gate-level bit-flip noise over 6 rounds without flag fault-tolerance, incurring deeper depth-10 syndrome circuits and thickness 3 embeddings.

Tools

Algebraic structure theory of 2BGA codes · Bit-mask exhaustive verifier · BP-OSD decoding · Circuit-level stabilizer extraction simulation

Abstract

Bivariate bicycle (BB) codes of Bravyi emphet al.~citeBravyi2024 are quantum low-density parity-check codes with weight-6 checks, exemplified by [[144,12,12]] with kd²/n=12. We develop the algebraic structure theory of BB-type codes with weight-8 checks (weight-4 generator polynomials) and use it, together with an exactly validated search pipeline, to construct and certify new codes. We prove an exact dimension formula k=2dimR/(A,B) (forcing even k), a 4ℓm-element symmetry group on generator pairs, an X/Z distance equality d_X=d_Z, and a family of subgroup-coset kernel vectors giving rigorous distance upper bounds and a design rule for high-distance constructions; all distances are computed exhaustively by a cross-validated bit-mask verifier. At n=144 the pipeline returns a census of 53 codes whose strongest members surpass the BB benchmark: [[144,6,d≥15]] exceeds the benchmark distance 12 (certified d≥15), [[144,10,12]] reaches it with weight-8 checks, and [[144,16,10]] encodes a third more logical qubits at kd²/n=11.11 (7.4% below benchmark) while decoding no worse. At n=72, [[72,14,8]] attains kd²/n=12.44---more than twice the same-length BB code---and decodes better; a circuit-level memory experiment places our weight-8 codes at ≈0.1% pseudo-threshold versus ≈0.4% for the BB reference under an identical model, quantifying the threshold cost of the heavier checks. All structural statements are verified numerically on the whole census.
